strengths: Solid theoretical foundation: the paper derives a sufficient-and-necessary condition (Thm 3.2) for the optimal low-rank update via truncated SVD of the gradient, then provides two tractable closed-form relaxations (scalar scaling in Thm 3.5, column-wise scaling in Thm 3.7) that avoid both the SVD cost and the need to reset adaptive-optimizer moment estimators, which is a genuine technical advance over ReLoRA (restart-based) and connects LoRA-GA as a special case.

The method is well motivated by concrete, previously identified shortcomings of high-rank LoRA variants (ReLoRA's restart overhead, MoRA's ad-hoc nonlinear compression, HiRA's O(mn) memory cost from Hadamard backprop), and the paper offers a clear complexity/memory analysis showing ScaLoRA(-I) compares favorably.

Extensive empirical validation across model scales (184M DeBERTaV3 to 12B Gemma-3) and task families (GLUE, 8 commonsense reasoning datasets, MetaMath/GSM8K/MATH), with consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over LoRA, MoRA, HiRA, ReLoRA, and LoRA-GA.

Careful ablations and diagnostics: verification of the rank(∇ℓ)≥2r assumption, empirical rate of positivity for the linear system in Thm 3.7, rank/stable-rank analysis of accumulated updates versus baselines, ablation on interval I, and scalar-only vs. column-wise scaling ablation, all of which help substantiate the theoretical claims with empirical evidence.
Reasonably transparent discussion of limitations (storage overhead, escalated per-step compute cost relative to LoRA) and a mitigation strategy (ScaLoRA-I) with a reported time/memory trade-off.
weaknesses: The globally optimal column-wise scaling (Thm 3.7) only applies when a 2r×2r linear system yields a non-negative solution, which the authors report holds in roughly 80% of layers/iterations; the remaining cases fall back to a different (scalar) scheme with no formal justification that the resulting mixture strategy retains any global optimality guarantee, somewhat undercutting the 'rigorous performance guarantees' framing in the abstract.

The core derivation relies on minimizing a majorizing quadratic upper bound of the loss (via the L-smoothness assumption) rather than the true loss; while common in optimization, the connection between minimizing this per-step surrogate and actual downstream task performance is asserted rather than rigorously established, and L is treated as a tuned hyperparameter, weakening the 'optimal' terminology used throughout.

The performance gains over strong high-rank baselines (HiRA, MoRA, LoRA-GA) are frequently small (e.g., ~0.5% average on GLUE, ~0.5-1% on commonsense reasoning) and often within one standard deviation of the reported error bars, raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement despite the added complexity.

Per-step time complexity O(mnr) is of the same order as the low-rank forward/backward pass itself, and Figure 3 shows ScaLoRA incurs 50%+ additional wall-clock time versus LoRA without the -I variant; while ScaLoRA-I amortizes this, its benefit is empirically tied to the (largely heuristic) choice of interval I, and the ablation (Table 10) shows a noticeable accuracy/loss trade-off as I grows.

ScaLoRA requires storing the full merged weight matrix per layer rather than only the small adapters, which the paper dismisses as inconsequential due to abundant disk space, but this changes the deployment/multi-tenant story that makes LoRA attractive in the first place (e.g., swapping/stacking many lightweight adapters), and this trade-off is not empirically explored.

Some relevant recent baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., DoRA, PiSSA, AdaLoRA-style budget allocation) are not included in the main experimental comparisons, and MoRA/HiRA are dropped from the largest-scale (12B) experiments due to scalability limits, leaving the strongest baselines untested at the largest model size where the method's practical value would be most impactful.
